definition: A molecular biology technique used to amplify a specific segment of DNA. Widely used in diagnostics to detect pathogens and genetic variants.
A PCR-based technique that quantifies the amount of a target DNA or RNA in real time using fluorescent reporters. Also called real-time PCR.
A digital PCR method that partitions a sample into thousands of droplets to enable absolute quantification of nucleic acids without a standard curve.
The molecule that carries the genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth, and reproduction of all known living organisms.
A molecule essential in gene expression and regulation. Includes mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA subtypes that participate in protein synthesis.
High-throughput DNA sequencing technology that enables rapid sequencing of entire genomes or targeted gene panels. Used in oncology diagnostics, infectious disease, and rare disease.
The process of determining the complete DNA sequence of an organism's genome. Used in outbreak investigations, oncology, and rare disease diagnosis.
A variation at a single position in a DNA sequence among individuals. SNPs are used as biomarkers in genetic disease studies and pharmacogenomics.
A cytogenetic technique using fluorescent probes that bind to specific chromosomal regions. Used to detect gene amplifications, deletions, and translocations.
A plate-based assay technique designed for detecting and quantifying substances such as peptides, proteins, antibodies, and hormones.
An immunoassay technique that uses chemiluminescent labels to detect analytes. Offers high sensitivity and is widely used on automated analyzers.
A paper-based point-of-care diagnostic device that detects target analytes via antibody-antigen interaction. Used in rapid tests for infectious diseases and pregnancy.
The most abundant antibody isotype in human blood. Provides long-term immunity and is used as a marker of past infection or vaccination response.
The first antibody produced in response to an infection. Elevated IgM typically indicates acute or recent infection.
An acute-phase protein produced by the liver in response to inflammation. Used as a biomarker for infection, inflammatory disease, and cardiovascular risk.
A measure of average blood glucose levels over the preceding 2–3 months. Standard diagnostic and monitoring test for diabetes mellitus.
A protein produced by prostate gland cells. Used as a screening biomarker for prostate cancer and to monitor treatment response.
A cardiac biomarker released into the bloodstream when heart muscle is damaged. High-sensitivity troponin assays are the gold standard for myocardial infarction diagnosis.
Lipoprotein that transports cholesterol in the blood. Elevated LDL is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
Cell-free tumour-derived DNA fragments found in the bloodstream. Used as a liquid biopsy biomarker for cancer detection and monitoring.
A biomarker measuring the total number of somatic mutations per megabase in a tumour genome. High TMB predicts response to immunotherapy.
A protein expressed on tumour cells that binds to the PD-1 receptor on T cells to suppress immune responses. A companion diagnostic target for checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
A peptide of 36–43 amino acids that is the main component of amyloid plaques in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease.
A microtubule-associated protein that becomes hyperphosphorylated in tauopathies such as Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia.
A lipoprotein involved in lipid transport. The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease.
An analytical technique that measures the mass-to-charge ratio of ions. Used to identify and quantify molecules in complex biological samples.
A non-invasive imaging technique using strong magnetic fields and radio waves to generate detailed images of organs and tissues without ionising radiation.
An imaging modality that uses X-rays and computer processing to create cross-sectional images of the body. Also known as a CAT scan.
A nuclear medicine functional imaging technique that produces 3D images of metabolic processes. Commonly combined with CT (PET-CT) for oncology staging.
The lowest amount of an analyte that can be reliably distinguished from the absence of that analyte. A fundamental analytical performance characteristic.
The lowest concentration at which an analyte can be quantitatively determined with acceptable precision and accuracy. Typically higher than the LOD.
The range of analyte concentrations that a method can directly measure without any modification. Equivalent to the reportable range in clinical chemistry.
A measure of relative precision expressed as the ratio of standard deviation to the mean, usually as a percentage. Used to compare assay variability across different concentration levels.
The ability of a test to correctly identify individuals with the target condition (true positive rate). Calculated as TP / (TP + FN).
The ability of a test to correctly identify individuals without the target condition (true negative rate). Calculated as TN / (TN + FP).
The probability that a person with a positive test result truly has the condition. Dependent on test sensitivity, specificity, and disease prevalence.
The probability that a person with a negative test result truly does not have the condition. Dependent on test sensitivity, specificity, and disease prevalence.
A graphical plot of diagnostic test sensitivity versus 1-specificity at various threshold settings. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarises overall discriminatory ability.
A measure of a diagnostic test's discriminatory ability derived from the ROC curve. Ranges from 0.5 (no discrimination) to 1.0 (perfect discrimination).
Materials and procedures used to monitor assay performance and detect systematic or random errors before patient results are reported.
External quality assessment program in which samples are distributed to multiple laboratories to assess the comparability of results. Required for laboratory accreditation.
Medical devices and accessories intended to be used in vitro for examination of specimens derived from the human body.
EU Regulation 2017/746 replacing the former IVD Directive. Introduces stricter requirements for clinical evidence, post-market surveillance, and notified body review for IVDs.
EU Regulation 2017/745 governing the placing on the market and putting into service of medical devices in the European Union.
United States federal agency responsible for protecting public health by regulating medical devices, drugs, and biologics.
The European Union agency responsible for the scientific evaluation, supervision, and safety monitoring of medicines for human and veterinary use.
CE marking indicates that a product meets EU safety, health, and environmental requirements. Required for IVD devices sold in the European Economic Area.
Documentation that accompanies a medical device explaining intended purpose, correct use, contraindications, warnings, and precautions.
A system for assigning a unique code to medical devices to improve traceability across the supply chain. Required under EU MDR/IVDR and FDA regulations.
A document in which the manufacturer states that a product conforms to all applicable EU regulations, enabling CE marking.
A proactive system for collecting and reviewing experience gained from medical devices placed on the market. Required under EU MDR and IVDR.
A continuous process of evaluating clinical data from a marketed device to confirm safety, performance, and clinical benefit. Part of PMS under EU MDR.
The EU central database for registration and transparency of medical devices, clinical investigations, certificates, and vigilance data.
A set of principles that ensure the quality and integrity of non-clinical laboratory studies submitted to regulatory authorities.
International body that brings together regulatory authorities and pharmaceutical industry to harmonise technical requirements for pharmaceutical products.
A documented step-by-step instruction for carrying out routine operations consistently. Required for quality management in laboratory settings.
A process for investigating root causes of non-conformances and implementing actions to prevent recurrence or occurrence. Core to ISO 13485 QMS.
A system of regulations for ensuring that products are consistently produced and controlled according to quality standards. Required for medical device manufacturers.
An organized system of documented processes, procedures, and responsibilities for achieving quality policies and objectives. ISO 13485 is the standard for medical device QMS.
A compilation of records that describes the design history of a finished device. Required under FDA 21 CFR Part 820.
Records demonstrating that a device was manufactured in accordance with the Device Master Record (DMR). Required under FDA 21 CFR Part 820.
A compilation of records containing the procedures and specifications for a finished device. The manufacturing equivalent of a recipe book.
A formal document raised when a product, process, or service fails to meet specified requirements. Typically triggers a CAPA process.
A test result that falls outside established acceptance criteria. Requires investigation and documented disposition before the product can be released or rejected.
Lowest analyte level a method can detect with a defined probability under specified conditions.
Lowest analyte level that can be quantified with predefined acceptable precision and bias.
Upper expected limit of results from blank samples under a defined statistical procedure.
Ability to detect small amounts of the intended analyte; often characterized by detection capability.
Ability to detect or measure the intended analyte without unacceptable cross-reactivity or interference.
Proportion of people with the target condition who test positive in a defined study population.
Proportion of people without the target condition who test negative in a defined study population.
Proportion of positive results that are true positives in the tested population; depends on prevalence.
Proportion of negative results that are true negatives in the tested population; depends on prevalence.
Proportion of comparator-positive specimens that test positive by the candidate method when a definitive gold standard is not used.
Proportion of comparator-negative specimens that test negative by the candidate method when a definitive gold standard is not used.
Proportion of specimens for which candidate and comparator classifications match.
Ratio of the probability of a positive result in people with the condition to that in people without it.
Ratio of the probability of a negative result in people with the condition to that in people without it.
Curve showing sensitivity versus false-positive rate across diagnostic thresholds.
Summary measure of discrimination, often calculated from a ROC curve.
An interval expressing uncertainty around an estimate under a specified statistical method.
Precision under the same operating conditions over a short interval.
Precision under changed conditions such as different sites, operators, instruments, or time periods.
Systematic difference between a measurement result and an accepted reference value.
Parameter describing the dispersion of values reasonably attributable to a measured quantity.
Range of results expected for a defined reference population and method; distinct from a clinical decision limit.
Threshold associated with a defined clinical action or risk category; not necessarily a population reference interval.
Operation establishing the relationship between instrument response and assigned calibrator values.
Material with an assigned value used to establish or verify measurement response.
Routine controls used to monitor analytical performance over time.
External comparison program used to evaluate laboratory performance against peers or assigned targets.
Control chart plotting QC results over time against a mean and standard-deviation limits.
Statistical decision rules used to interpret QC results and detect potential analytical errors.
Processes before measurement, including collection, labeling, transport, and specimen preparation.
Stage in which the specimen is measured or analyzed.
Processes after measurement, including review, reporting, interpretation, and communication.
Defined conditions under which a specimen is unsuitable for testing, such as mislabeling or inadequate volume.
Documented control of a specimen from collection through transfer, testing, storage, and disposition.
Rupture of red blood cells releasing intracellular contents that may interfere with selected measurements.
Excess lipid particles that cause turbidity and may interfere with some methods.
Bilirubin-associated sample coloration that may interfere with some assays depending on method and concentration.
Hematology panel including red cells, white cells, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelets.
Average red blood cell volume, used in classifying anemia.
Number of platelets in a defined blood volume.
Coagulation test assessing selected clotting pathways; commonly used in anticoagulation monitoring.
Standardized expression of prothrombin time, particularly for vitamin K antagonist monitoring.
Coagulation test used to assess selected clotting pathways and support evaluation of bleeding disorders or heparin therapy.
Common chemistry panel including selected electrolytes, glucose, and kidney-related measurements; contents vary by setting.
Chemistry panel including electrolytes, glucose, kidney-related and selected liver/protein measurements.
Blood or urine analyte used with other information to assess kidney function.
Estimate of kidney filtration calculated using a validated equation and patient measurements.
Enzyme measured in blood as a marker of liver cell injury.
Enzyme that may increase with liver, muscle, or other tissue injury; AST also means antimicrobial susceptibility testing in microbiology.
Enzyme measured in selected evaluations of hepatobiliary and bone conditions.
Acute-phase protein measured as a nonspecific marker of inflammation.
Biomarker that may support evaluation of bacterial infection in selected contexts; not definitive alone.
Measurement reflecting average glycemia over roughly the preceding two to three months, with known interpretive limitations.
Pituitary hormone commonly measured as an initial test of thyroid function.
Urine assessment that may include physical appearance, chemical strip testing, and microscopy.
Culture-based test to detect and identify organisms in urine.
Blood incubated in culture media to detect bloodstream infection; collection technique affects contamination risk.
Workflow that grows an organism, identifies it, and tests susceptibility to selected antimicrobials.
Testing that determines how an isolate responds to antimicrobial agents. In chemistry, AST can also mean aspartate aminotransferase.
Lowest antimicrobial concentration preventing visible microbial growth under specified test conditions.
Interpretive threshold used to categorize susceptibility for a defined organism, drug, method, and standard version.
Ability of a microorganism to survive or grow despite exposure to an antimicrobial that would ordinarily inhibit it.
Mass-spectrometry method used to identify microorganisms from characteristic protein profiles.
Differential staining method that broadly classifies bacteria by staining characteristics and morphology.
Staining method used to detect acid-fast organisms, including mycobacteria, in appropriate specimens.
Unit estimating viable microorganisms capable of forming colonies under defined culture conditions.
Method in which RNA is converted to complementary DNA before amplification; distinct from real-time PCR despite common naming confusion.
Control included in a test workflow to monitor selected steps such as extraction, amplification, or detection.
Control used to monitor nucleic-acid extraction and help identify extraction failures or contamination.
PCR control with no target nucleic acid, used to detect contamination in reagents or reaction setup.
PCR cycle at which fluorescence crosses a defined threshold; interpretation and comparison are assay-dependent.
Measure of how effectively target nucleic acid is amplified during each PCR cycle.
Analysis of fluorescence during controlled heating to assess amplification product characteristics in selected PCR methods.
Diagnostic test detecting target DNA or RNA using amplification or related molecular methods.
Nucleic-acid amplification method performed at a constant temperature using multiple primers.
Rapid test format in which a liquid sample migrates along a membrane and produces a visible or instrument-read signal.
Testing performed near the patient rather than solely in a central laboratory.
Immunoassay using a chemiluminescent reaction to generate a measurable signal.
Immunoassay measuring light generated by an electrochemically initiated luminescence reaction.
Test designed to detect a component of a pathogen or other target, often through immunochemical recognition.
Test detecting antibodies; results may reflect prior exposure, vaccination, or current immune response depending on context.
Antibody class often produced early in an immune response; interpretation depends on assay and clinical context.
Antibody class commonly associated with longer-term immune responses; a positive result does not alone establish timing or active infection.
Autoantibody test used in evaluating selected systemic autoimmune diseases; a positive result is not diagnostic by itself.
Antibody measurement that may support evaluation of rheumatoid arthritis and other conditions but is not disease-specific.
Technique measuring physical or fluorescent characteristics of individual cells or particles as they pass through an instrument.
Method using antibodies to detect specific antigens in tissue sections.
Study or diagnostic examination of individual cells or cell samples.
Microscopic examination of tissue to assess disease-related structural changes.
Test essential for safe and effective use of a corresponding therapeutic product in the intended patient population.
Tumor-derived DNA fragments found in blood or other body fluids and studied for selected cancer applications.
Genetic variant for which available evidence is insufficient to classify as benign or pathogenic under a defined framework.
Proportion of sequencing reads at a genomic position that contain a specified variant.
Genomic alteration involving deletion or duplication of DNA segments relative to a reference genome.
Sequencing focused on protein-coding regions of the genome for selected genetic investigations.
Sequencing assay designed to analyze a defined set of genes associated with a disease or clinical question.
Process of identifying candidate genomic differences from sequencing data relative to a reference sequence.
Representative genome sequence used as a coordinate framework for aligning and interpreting sequencing data.
Number of sequencing reads covering a genomic position or region, used to assess coverage and confidence.
Evidence that a method meets predefined analytical performance requirements for its intended use.
Evidence that a test's performance supports its intended clinical use in the target population and setting.
Documented confirmation that a method or system meets specified requirements in the user's setting.
Purpose, target population, user, specimen, setting, and clinical role for which a diagnostic product is designed and evaluated.
Manufacturer-provided information describing intended use, operating procedures, limitations, warnings, and other required information.
Medical device intended to examine human-derived specimens to provide diagnostic, monitoring, or related information.
Designation for products intended for research use and not diagnostic procedures; it does not itself establish regulatory compliance.
Labeling designation for products being investigated and not represented for routine diagnostic use; exact rules depend on jurisdiction.
Structured process for planning, documenting, reviewing, verifying, and validating medical-device design activities.
Systematic identification, evaluation, control, and monitoring of risks throughout a device lifecycle.
Process for analyzing and reducing use-related risks and supporting safe and effective device use.
Software intended for medical purposes that performs those purposes without being part of a hardware medical device.
Objective evidence that design outputs meet specified design input requirements.
Objective evidence that a device meets user needs and intended uses under defined conditions.
Documented process for evaluating, approving, implementing, and reviewing changes to products, processes, software, or documents.
Structured mapping between requirements and related design, risk, verification, validation, and test evidence.
Documented process for receiving, evaluating, investigating, and responding to product complaints.
Activities to collect and evaluate information about a device after market placement.
System for identifying medical devices through device and production identifiers, as applicable.
U.S. federal requirements governing many laboratories that test human specimens for health assessment or diagnosis, subject to scope and exemptions.
Organization that accredits laboratories and provides proficiency testing and laboratory quality programs.
Software used to manage laboratory workflows, orders, specimens, results, quality processes, and reporting.
Software used to track samples, workflows, results, and metadata, often in research or industrial laboratories.
HL7 standard for exchanging healthcare information using defined resources and modern web-based approaches.

term: Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes
definition: Terminology standard for identifying laboratory tests, clinical observations, and related measurements.

term: Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms
definition: Clinical terminology used to represent concepts consistently in electronic health information.
Electronic process or symbol used to sign a record, subject to applicable identity, intent, and record-control requirements.
U.S. FDA regulations addressing criteria for trustworthy and reliable electronic records and electronic signatures within their scope.
Identification and mitigation of cybersecurity risks affecting device safety, effectiveness, data integrity, or availability.
Chronological record of relevant system actions and changes supporting traceability and accountability.
source_reference: FDA electronic records guidance; QMS procedures

definition: Individually identifiable health information protected under applicable HIPAA rules when held or transmitted by covered entities or business associates.
Access-control approach granting permissions based on assigned roles and responsibilities.
Automated collection and transmission of instrument measurements and status data for monitoring or analysis.
Reliability metric representing average operating time between failures for a repairable system under stated assumptions.
Metric representing average time required to restore a failed system to operation; definition should be stated.
Planned maintenance intended to reduce failure likelihood and preserve instrument performance.
Software connecting laboratory analyzers with laboratory information systems and possibly routing results or applying rules.
Elapsed time between defined start and end points for a laboratory process, such as receipt to result release.
Additional testing automatically initiated when an initial result meets predefined criteria.
Result considered to indicate a potentially life-threatening condition and requiring prompt communication under laboratory policy.
Automated release of results meeting predefined rules and quality criteria without manual review of each result.
Study comparing results from a candidate method with a comparator method across suitable specimens.
Study designed to estimate variability under defined repeatability or reproducibility conditions.
Extent to which measured results are proportional to analyte concentration over a stated interval.
Documented check that a new reagent or consumable lot performs acceptably before routine use.
Documented evidence that a computerized system is fit for intended use and meets applicable requirements.
Inventory of software components and dependencies included in a product, supporting vulnerability and supply-chain risk management.
Completeness, consistency, accuracy, and reliability of data throughout its lifecycle.
Data integrity principles: attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, plus complete, consistent, enduring, and available.
Regulatory mechanism that may permit use of certain medical products during a declared emergency when statutory criteria are met.
U.S. FDA submission pathway for certain devices to demonstrate substantial equivalence to a legally marketed predicate.
U.S. FDA pathway requiring evidence of safety and effectiveness for certain higher-risk medical devices.
EU Regulation 2017/746 governing in vitro diagnostic medical devices, including classification, conformity assessment, and post-market obligations.
EU Regulation 2017/745 governing medical devices other than IVDs; MDR can have other meanings in laboratories.
Process demonstrating that a product meets applicable regulatory requirements before market placement or use.
Report documenting evidence for an IVD's performance evaluation under the applicable regulatory framework.
Body of information supporting clinical performance and clinical validity for a diagnostic product's intended purpose.
source_reference: FDA; EU IVDR; diagnostic evidence guidance

definition: Extent to which use of a test leads to improved health outcomes or meaningful clinical decisions in its intended context.
Method accepted as suitable for establishing a reference value or classification for a defined measurement or diagnostic comparison.
Method selected as a basis for comparison with a candidate test in a performance evaluation.
Statistical calculation estimating the number of specimens or participants needed for planned precision or power.
Method estimating the probability that a study detects a specified effect under its assumptions and design.
Proportion of a population with a condition at a specified time or during a defined period.
Bias arising when diagnostic performance is evaluated in a population unlike the intended-use population in severity or characteristics.
Bias occurring when the reference standard is applied differently depending on the index test result.
Study design practice keeping specified participants or assessors unaware of selected information to reduce bias.
Clinical evidence derived from analysis of real-world data, with strength depending on data quality and study design.
Data relating to health status or healthcare delivery collected from sources such as records, claims, registries, or devices.
Defined claim linking a diagnostic test to safe and effective use of a corresponding therapy in a specified population.
Quality system for nonclinical laboratory studies within its scope; distinct from clinical laboratory accreditation.
Ethical and scientific quality standards for designing, conducting, recording, and reporting clinical trials.
Practices supporting accurate, complete, attributable, legible, contemporaneous, and traceable records.
Structured investigation to identify underlying causes of a failure or nonconformance rather than only symptoms.
Prospective method for identifying potential failure modes, effects, and risk-reduction actions.

term: Failure mode, effects, and criticality analysis
definition: Extension of FMEA that also evaluates the criticality of potential failure modes.
Documented requirement defining what a medical device or system must do or satisfy.
Documented results of design activities evaluated against design inputs and used for production or service.
Approved plan specifying validation objectives, methods, acceptance criteria, responsibilities, and required records.
Predefined measurable conditions that results must satisfy for a test, verification, validation, or release decision to pass.
Failure to fulfill a specified requirement.
Activities for assessing, approving, monitoring, and controlling suppliers whose products or services affect quality.
Evidence that software implementation and outputs meet specified requirements and design specifications.
Evidence that software satisfies user needs and intended use in its specified environment.
Ability of systems or organizations to exchange information and use the information exchanged effectively.
Standards-development organization whose standards support exchange and integration of health information.
Digital system containing patient health information and clinical documentation used by authorized care teams.
Defined sequence of tests or decision rules used to interpret findings and determine next diagnostic steps.
Positive result in a person or specimen that does not have the target condition or analyte under the reference definition.
Negative result in a person or specimen that has the target condition or analyte under the reference definition.
Result that does not meet criteria for positive or negative interpretation and requires defined handling.
Result that fails predefined assay or system validity criteria and should not be interpreted as valid positive or negative.
Test used to identify people who may need further assessment; not necessarily diagnostic by itself.
Follow-up test used to establish or rule out an initial screening or preliminary result under a defined algorithm.
Group of viruses, some types associated with cervical and other cancers; testing is used in defined screening and diagnostic pathways.
Respiratory virus that can cause significant lower respiratory tract disease, especially in infants and older adults.
Coronavirus responsible for COVID-19; diagnostic methods include nucleic-acid amplification and antigen tests.
Viral antigen used in testing for hepatitis B infection as part of an appropriate serologic algorithm.
Antibody test used in screening for hepatitis C exposure; reactive results generally need follow-up testing for current infection.
Combined assay detecting HIV antigen and antibodies; follow-up follows the applicable diagnostic algorithm.
High-sensitivity measurement of CRP used in selected cardiovascular risk assessments and other contexts.
Biomarker used with clinical assessment to support evaluation of heart failure.
Biomarker used with clinical assessment to support evaluation of heart failure and related conditions.
Metabolite measured in blood or other specimens in selected evaluations of perfusion, metabolism, or critical illness.
Measurement of blood gas and acid-base parameters, often including pH, carbon dioxide, and oxygen-related values.
Urine ratio used to assess albuminuria, particularly in evaluation and monitoring of kidney disease.
Stool test detecting human hemoglobin using antibodies, commonly used in colorectal cancer screening programs.
Blood testing for selected antibodies used in evaluation of celiac disease, interpreted with clinical context and other criteria.
Coordinated interventions to improve appropriate antimicrobial use and limit resistance.
Infection acquired while receiving healthcare that was not present or incubating at admission under the applicable definition.
Containment practices and facility requirements appropriate to risks of work with specified biological agents or materials.
Equipment worn to reduce exposure to hazards, selected according to task and risk assessment.
Ventilated enclosure designed to provide defined levels of personnel, product, and environmental protection when used correctly.
Document describing chemical hazards, handling, storage, exposure controls, and emergency measures.
Classification of room air cleanliness based on airborne particle concentration limits and measurement methods.
Validated process intended to render a product free of viable microorganisms to a specified sterility assurance level.
Population of viable microorganisms present on or in a product before a defined microbial reduction or sterilization process.
Documented agreement defining service expectations and measurable commitments such as availability or response time.
Target maximum time to restore a service or system after disruption.
Target maximum acceptable data loss measured in time after a disruption.
Controlled document defining functional, performance, interface, and other software requirements.
Software item already developed and generally available whose development processes or records may not be known; term used in IEC 62304.
Defined interface through which software systems exchange data or invoke functions.
FHIR resource used to represent measurements and simple assertions, including many laboratory results.
FHIR resource representing a diagnostic report and potentially grouping observations and findings.
International standard specifying requirements for quality and competence in medical laboratories.
International standard specifying quality management system requirements for organizations involved in medical devices.
International standard describing application of risk management to medical devices throughout their lifecycle.
Standard defining software lifecycle processes for medical device software.
Standard addressing usability engineering for medical devices, including analysis and mitigation of use-related risks.
Standard specifying requirements for point-of-care testing and intended to be used with ISO 15189.
Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, which develops standards and guidelines used in laboratory medicine and diagnostic testing.
European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing, developing methods and breakpoint tables for susceptibility interpretation.
Guidelines describing minimum information to report for quantitative real-time PCR experiments to improve transparency and reproducibility.
aliases: Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments

definition: FDA quality management system regulation for medical devices, aligned substantially with ISO 13485:2016; check current FDA guidance for applicability and dates.
Activities to proactively collect and evaluate performance data for an IVD after market placement under applicable IVDR requirements.
Study designed to establish or confirm analytical or clinical performance of an in vitro diagnostic device.
Evidence supporting association between an analyte or marker and a clinical condition or physiological state for a defined purpose.
Automated transmission of reportable laboratory results from laboratories to public health agencies in a defined format.
source_reference: CDC; HL7 public health reporting references

definition: Managed set of deployed diagnostic instruments tracked for status, location, maintenance, software version, and service history.
source_reference: Asset management and service operations references

definition: Periodic signal indicating that a device or service is communicating and responsive.
Condition in which an expected heartbeat is not received within a defined interval.
Defined state describing equipment availability or condition, such as ready, running, maintenance, or error.
Tracked record of a reported service request or problem, including owner, status, priority, and resolution.
Proportion of service incidents resolved during the initial service visit or intervention without a follow-up visit for the same issue.
Service outcome in which no reproducible fault is identified under the diagnostic procedures performed.
Manufacturer action to prevent or reduce the risk of a serious incident involving a device already made available on the market.
Manufacturer communication to customers or users describing a field safety corrective action and relevant instructions.
Compilation of records describing the design history of a finished device under applicable quality-system requirements.
Records demonstrating that a finished device or lot was manufactured according to applicable manufacturing requirements.
Compilation of records containing procedures and specifications for manufacturing a finished device.
Formal record describing failure to meet requirements and its assessment, disposition, and associated actions.
Result outside established acceptance criteria or specifications, requiring documented investigation and disposition.
Result within specification but deviating from an expected pattern or historical trend, potentially requiring investigation.
Material expected to produce a positive result, used to demonstrate specified assay functions are working.
Material expected to produce a negative result, used to help detect contamination or nonspecific reactivity.
Target or control sequence included to indicate whether amplification and detection proceeded adequately.
Substance in a specimen or reagent that reduces amplification efficiency or prevents a valid PCR reaction.
Process isolating DNA or RNA from a specimen while removing substances that may inhibit downstream analysis.
Short nucleic-acid sequence providing a starting point for DNA synthesis in amplification or sequencing workflows.
Labeled or otherwise detectable molecule designed to bind a target sequence or analyte.
DNA or RNA-derived fragment produced by an amplification process.
PCR approach partitioning a sample into many reactions and estimating target concentration from positive partitions.
Change at a single nucleotide position in a genome; the term describes an observed sequence difference regardless of population frequency.
Genetic variant involving insertion or deletion of one or more nucleotides relative to a reference sequence.
Genomic alteration involving larger-scale changes such as deletions, duplications, inversions, or translocations.
Measure of somatic mutations in a defined amount of tumor genomic sequence, with assay-specific methods and thresholds.
Length changes in short repetitive DNA sequences due to impaired mismatch repair, used in selected cancer evaluations.
Loss or dysfunction of DNA mismatch repair proteins or activity, assessed in selected cancer diagnostic workflows.
Protein and gene target assessed in selected cancers to support classification and treatment decisions.
Receptor assessed in selected breast cancer pathology workflows to support tumor characterization and treatment decisions.
Receptor assessed in selected breast cancer pathology workflows to support tumor characterization and treatment decisions.
Cellular proliferation marker assessed by immunohistochemistry in selected pathology contexts.
Fluorescently labeled nucleic-acid probe designed to hybridize to a specific chromosome or genomic region.
Method for detecting copy-number changes and selected genomic imbalances across the genome.
Description or image of an individual's chromosomes arranged by number, size, and morphology.
Screening of newborns for selected conditions under a defined public health program and follow-up algorithm.
Specimen prepared by applying blood to filter paper and drying it for selected testing and storage workflows.
Analysis of cell-free DNA in maternal blood to screen for selected fetal chromosomal conditions; screening is not diagnostic confirmation.
Mass spectrometry technique using sequential mass analysis stages, used in selected newborn screening and biochemical testing.
Chemical strip test used to screen urine for selected analytes or characteristics.
Measure related to urine density compared with water, used as an indicator of concentration.
Urine strip test detecting an enzyme associated with white blood cells, used as one indicator of inflammation or infection.
Test that detects hidden blood in stool; method types and recommended uses differ.
Protein measured in blood that may support evaluation or monitoring of prostate conditions; not specific for cancer.
Protein measured in blood that can be used with validated equations to estimate glomerular filtration.
Measurement of urea nitrogen in blood, used with other information to assess kidney function and metabolic status.
Average platelet size in a blood sample, interpreted with other hematology findings and method limitations.
Measure of variation in red blood cell size, used with other indices in evaluating anemia.
Calculated or measured number of neutrophils in a blood volume, used in selected infection-risk assessments.
Fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord analyzed for infectious, inflammatory, malignant, or other conditions.
Fluid from a joint that may be analyzed for cells, crystals, and microorganisms in selected conditions.
Fluid from the space around the lungs analyzed for selected chemical, microbiological, or cytological purposes.
Culture-based test used to recover and help identify fungi from an appropriate clinical specimen.
Testing designed to detect mycoplasma contamination in relevant biological materials, cell cultures, or manufacturing processes.
Enzyme that hydrolyzes carbapenem antibiotics and can contribute to clinically important antimicrobial resistance.
Enzyme that can confer resistance to many penicillins and cephalosporins; interpretation follows organism-specific guidance.
Staphylococcus aureus with resistance to methicillin and related beta-lactam antibiotics under applicable criteria.
Enterococcus species classified as resistant to vancomycin under applicable susceptibility criteria.
Lowest antimicrobial concentration that kills a defined proportion of bacterial inoculum under specified conditions.
Gradient diffusion method used to estimate the MIC of an antimicrobial agent for a microorganism.
Standardized antimicrobial susceptibility method interpreting inhibition-zone diameters using defined criteria.
Summary of antimicrobial susceptibility patterns for organisms isolated in a defined population and period.
Multiplex test panel designed to detect multiple potential causes associated with a clinical syndrome.
Diagnostic panel testing for selected respiratory pathogens; targets and performance vary by product.
Diagnostic panel detecting selected pathogens and sometimes resistance markers in blood or positive blood-culture material.
Test response caused by a non-intended substance or target due to shared or similar recognition features.
Assay phenomenon in which very high analyte concentrations produce unexpectedly low signal or result in some immunoassays.
Interference from antibodies binding assay reagents nonspecifically and causing erroneous immunoassay results.
Interference in assays using biotin-streptavidin chemistry when biotin alters assay signal or result.
Influence from sample components that alters measurement response or assay performance.
Extent to which a reference material behaves like patient samples across measurement procedures.
Material sufficiently homogeneous and stable for use in measurement or examination of specified properties.
Reference material with documentation from an authoritative body providing property values and associated uncertainty and traceability.
Property of a measurement result related to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations.
Measurement-system study estimating variation associated with equipment and appraisers under a defined design.
source_reference: AIAG MSA; measurement system analysis references

definition: Evaluation of a measurement process's variation, bias, stability, linearity, and other characteristics.
